context.concept_name: Handle failed event delivery with bounded retries and failure capture

required_facts.statement: EventBridge retries retryable target-delivery failures within configured maximum event age and retry-attempt limits.
Configure the target RetryPolicy MaximumRetryAttempts and MaximumEventAgeInSeconds to the approved finite budget.
Configure DeadLetterConfig with the approved SQS queue ARN and required queue permissions, then inspect a seeded exhausted delivery failure in that queue.
Some nonretryable delivery failures go directly to failure capture; retry configuration does not guarantee every failure receives retries.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An event reaches a target that cannot accept it. Configure a finite retry budget and failure capture so the supplied delivery failure can be inspected instead of disappearing into indefinite retries.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: EventBridge retries retryable target-delivery failures within configured maximum event age and retry-attempt limits.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Configure the target RetryPolicy MaximumRetryAttempts and MaximumEventAgeInSeconds to the approved finite budget.

Configure DeadLetterConfig with the approved SQS queue ARN and required queue permissions, then inspect a seeded exhausted delivery failure in that queue.

Some nonretryable delivery failures go directly to failure capture; retry configuration does not guarantee every failure receives retries.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Set RetryPolicy MaximumRetryAttempts and MaximumEventAgeInSeconds to the approved finite limits. Configure DeadLetterConfig with the approved SQS queue ARN and required queue permissions. Inspect the seeded exhausted-delivery failure in that queue and retain its evidence. Retryable target-delivery failures are retried within both age and attempt limits. Some nonretryable failures go directly to capture, so do not expect every failure to exhibit the full retry sequence. The example verifies the bounded policy and captured failure together; merely configuring a retry count does not prove that the capture queue can accept or holds the supplied failed event.

Compare the supplied retryable-exhaustion case with a captured nonretryable failure. The first should be interpreted against finite age and attempt limits; the latter need not show a full retry history. Both require inspectable capture evidence at the approved queue. Required queue permissions are part of that route, so a configured ARN alone cannot be substituted for the actual captured-event check.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Retry configuration does not guarantee that every failure receives retries. Some nonretryable failures go directly to capture. Also, a configured dead-letter queue requires the required permissions and inspection of the seeded failure to verify capture.

video_need.reason: Finite retry attempts, event age and captured delivery failures benefit from a delivery timeline with the nonretryable branch shown.

practice_anchor.objective: Configure one supplied EventBridge target with the approved MaximumRetryAttempts and MaximumEventAgeInSeconds values, then configure DeadLetterConfig with the approved SQS queue ARN and required queue permissions. Inspect the seeded exhausted delivery failure in that queue.
practice_anchor.success: The target's retry policy matches both approved finite limits, and its dead-letter configuration and queue permissions allow failure capture. The seeded exhausted event is inspectable in the approved queue, and the supplied delivery evidence is consistent with the configured retry budget.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show a retryable target-delivery failure progressing through retries bounded by maximum event age and retry attempts, then reaching the approved SQS failure-capture queue when the budget is exhausted. Show a separate nonretryable branch going directly to capture, with queue permissions and inspection of the captured event identified as required checks.

teaching_notes: Use supplied finite limits and SQS queue; do not invent retry intervals or guaranteed retry causes.

context.concept_name: Perform a controlled ECS service rollout

required_facts.statement: An ECS rolling deployment replaces service tasks according to minimumHealthyPercent and maximumPercent relative to desiredCount.
Register the supplied new image version in a task-definition revision and update the service to that revision.
Inspect service events, running task revisions and health until the supplied steady-state criteria are met; a service-update request alone is not proof of a healthy rollout.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An ECS service needs a new image revision without treating the update request as proof of a healthy rollout. Read the supplied replacement bounds and observe service/task health until steady-state criteria pass.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: An ECS rolling deployment replaces service tasks according to minimumHealthyPercent and maximumPercent relative to desiredCount.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Register the supplied new image version in a task-definition revision and update the service to that revision.

Inspect service events, running task revisions and health until the supplied steady-state criteria are met; a service-update request alone is not proof of a healthy rollout.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Register the supplied new image in a task-definition revision and update the service to it. Inspect service events, running task revisions and health against the supplied criteria. minimumHealthyPercent and maximumPercent describe replacement bounds relative to desiredCount. Keep those settings with the observations rather than assuming every rolling update replaces all tasks at once. Stop calling the rollout complete at the update request; verify the supplied steady state.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Service-update acceptance is not a healthy rollout result. Verify events, running revisions and health until the supplied steady-state criteria are met, using the configured percent bounds relative to desiredCount.

video_need.reason: Changing task revisions, replacement bounds and eventual steady-state health benefit from a short ECS service rollout demonstration.

practice_anchor.objective: Roll one supplied ECS service from image version A to B by registering a task-definition revision and updating the service, then verify task health against the supplied steady-state criteria.
practice_anchor.success: The service uses the registered version B task-definition revision. Observed task replacement is consistent with the supplied minimumHealthyPercent and maximumPercent relative to desiredCount, and service events, running task revisions and health satisfy every supplied steady-state criterion.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the service's desiredCount, replacement percentage bounds, selected task-definition revision, service events, running task revisions and health visible during replacement and at the verified steady state.

teaching_notes: Use supplied task definition and steady-state checks; do not add load-driven ECS scaling.

context.concept_name: Promote the same artifact version across environments

coverage.learning_objective: Promote the same artifact version across environments

required_facts.statement: The build stage produces a build artifact; release combines that build with environment configuration, and run executes the release.
Promote the same immutable artifact reference or digest to the next environment while supplying that environment’s configuration rather than rebuilding the source.
Compare the deployed artifact digests in staging and production and their recorded build provenance to verify the tested output is the promoted output.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A staging-tested release should promote the same built content to the next environment. Change the supplied environment configuration without rebuilding the source into a different output.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: The build stage produces a build artifact; release combines that build with environment configuration, and run executes the release.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Promote the same immutable artifact reference or digest to the next environment while supplying that environment’s configuration rather than rebuilding the source.

Compare the deployed artifact digests in staging and production and their recorded build provenance to verify the tested output is the promoted output.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Carry the same immutable artifact reference or digest from staging to production and supply production's approved configuration. Compare deployed digests in both environments and their recorded build provenance. If the digests differ, the evidence does not show that the tested output was promoted. Build produces the artifact, release combines it with environment configuration, and run executes that release.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Rebuilding from the same source is not this same-artifact promotion check. Promote the immutable reference/digest and verify deployed digests with build provenance; environment configuration belongs to the release combination.

video_need.reason: A short environment/digest/provenance comparison helps verify same-content promotion without a new build demonstration.

practice_anchor.objective: Promote the supplied staging artifact to production by retaining its immutable reference or digest and selecting the supplied production configuration, without creating a new build.
practice_anchor.success: Production uses the supplied production configuration and the same immutable artifact as staging. The deployed staging and production digests match, their recorded build provenance identifies the same build output, and no rebuild occurs.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show staging and production side by side with their immutable artifact references, deployed digests, recorded build provenance, and environment configuration, making the shared build output and environment-specific configuration visible.

teaching_notes: Use supplied artifact and environment configuration; do not create a new build during promotion.

required_facts.statement: Cost Explorer data is refreshed at least once every 24 hours and some data can take longer to appear.
Inspect the supplied teardown interval with account and service or usage-type filters and compare usage timestamps with resource-deletion evidence.
Distinguish charges for usage before deletion from evidence of continuing usage and repeat the check after the billing data refresh rather than declaring zero cost from resource absence.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: Teardown removed resources, but the bill still needs a time-aware check. Cost Explorer may report older usage after deletion, and an absence of resources is not a zero-cost result.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: Cost Explorer data is refreshed at least once every 24 hours and some data can take longer to appear.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Inspect the supplied teardown interval with account and service or usage-type filters and compare usage timestamps with resource-deletion evidence.

Distinguish charges for usage before deletion from evidence of continuing usage and repeat the check after the billing data refresh rather than declaring zero cost from resource absence.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Filter the supplied teardown interval by account and service or usage type. Compare usage timestamps with resource-deletion evidence. A charge associated with usage before deletion is different from evidence of continuing usage after deletion. Record that timing distinction and repeat the check after the billing-data refresh. Cost Explorer refreshes at least once every 24 hours, and some data can take longer to appear. Do not declare zero cost solely because the resources are gone or the first post-teardown report is empty. This exercise verifies residual charges against deletion evidence and reporting delay rather than inventing a new price estimate.

If the first report has no charge in the teardown interval, retain that observation but label it as the current reporting result. Repeat after refresh before concluding about residual charges. If a later report adds usage, compare its usage timestamps with deletion evidence rather than assuming its appearance time is its usage time. This makes the conclusion about metered activity and reporting lag, not the time the operator opened the report.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: A charge appearing after deletion is not automatically proof of post-deletion usage. Compare usage timestamps and repeat after data refresh. Conversely, resource absence or an early empty report does not prove zero cost.

video_need.reason: A short usage-time/deletion-time comparison helps distinguish residual reporting from continuing usage; the billing-delay rules suffice in text.

practice_anchor.objective: Inspect supplied Cost Explorer usage and cost data for one teardown window using account and service or usage-type filters. Compare usage timestamps with supplied resource-deletion evidence, and repeat the inspection using a supplied refreshed report.
practice_anchor.success: The inspection uses the supplied interval and relevant filters, distinguishes pre-deletion usage charges from evidence of continuing usage after deletion, and records any empty initial result as provisional. The conclusion incorporates the refreshed report and acknowledges that Cost Explorer refreshes at least once every 24 hours while some data can take longer to appear.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the teardown interval, account, service or usage type, usage timestamps, costs, deletion evidence, and initial versus refreshed reporting results visible together so usage time can be distinguished from reporting time.

teaching_notes: Preserve at-least-daily refresh and possible longer appearance delay; do not promise a fixed final billing time.

coverage.learning_objective: Isolate access to S3 Terraform state

required_facts.statement: S3 backend access needs permissions for the selected state bucket and object key; state can contain sensitive values.
Scope approved readers and writers to the required ListBucket prefix and GetObject/PutObject state object operations, with supplied locking permissions configured separately.
Initialize the supplied backend, provision the separate exercise bucket through the approved identity, and test that an unapproved identity cannot read or overwrite state.
State access isolation prevents unauthorized access; it is separate from the mechanism that coordinates concurrent authorized writers.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: Remote Terraform state can contain sensitive values, so its reader/writer boundary needs its own access test. Backend access isolation is different from coordinating concurrent authorized writers.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: S3 backend access needs permissions for the selected state bucket and object key; state can contain sensitive values.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Scope approved readers and writers to the required ListBucket prefix and GetObject/PutObject state object operations, with supplied locking permissions configured separately.

Initialize the supplied backend, provision the separate exercise bucket through the approved identity, and test that an unapproved identity cannot read or overwrite state.

State access isolation prevents unauthorized access; it is separate from the mechanism that coordinates concurrent authorized writers.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Scope the supplied readers/writers to the required ListBucket prefix and GetObject/PutObject state-object operations. Configure supplied locking permissions separately. Initialize the intended backend and provision the separate exercise bucket through the approved identity. Test that the unapproved identity cannot read or overwrite state, recording those outcomes without exposing state content. The selected bucket/key access boundary protects sensitive state; locking serves a different coordination purpose.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Locking is not the state authorization boundary. State access isolation prevents unauthorized access, while a separate mechanism coordinates authorized writers. Test unapproved read and overwrite rather than assuming backend initialization proves isolation.

video_need.reason: A short authorized/unapproved state-access comparison helps locate the storage permission boundary separately from writer locking.

practice_anchor.objective: Configure scoped access to the supplied S3 state bucket, prefix, and object key. Using the approved identity and supplied Terraform configuration, initialize the backend and provision one separate S3 exercise bucket. Test that the unapproved identity cannot read or overwrite state, leaving the supplied coordination configuration unchanged.
practice_anchor.success: Approved readers have the required prefix-scoped ListBucket and state-object GetObject access; approved writers also have state-object PutObject access. The approved provisioning identity creates the separate exercise bucket with state stored in the supplied backend. Unapproved read and overwrite attempts are denied, and recorded evidence does not expose state contents.

live_code.required_skill: Edit a scoped IAM policy and execute supplied Terraform and S3 access checks using approved and unapproved operator profiles.
allowed_syntax: IAM policy JSON: Version, Statement, Effect, Action, Resource, Condition
s3:ListBucket with a supplied s3:prefix condition
s3:GetObject and s3:PutObject scoped to the supplied state object ARN
Supplied Terraform HCL backend, provider, and S3 exercise-bucket configuration
live_code.starter_state_intent: Provide an isolated S3 backend with a supplied bucket, prefix, and state key; approved and unapproved operator profiles; a scoped policy template; and a ready Terraform configuration for one separate S3 exercise bucket. Backend initialization instructions and writer-coordination permissions are supplied. Provide protected local output locations and a controlled unapproved overwrite probe.
live_code.observable_success: Policy inspection confirms prefix-scoped bucket listing and exact state-object read/write permissions for the intended identities. Approved initialization and provisioning succeed. The unapproved identity receives access-denied outcomes for both state retrieval and the controlled overwrite attempt; state remains unchanged by those tests, and evidence records outcomes rather than sensitive contents.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the selected state bucket, prefix, and object-key permission boundary visible alongside approved and unapproved read/write outcomes. Show separate exercise-bucket provisioning and distinguish state authorization from the supplied authorized-writer coordination mechanism without displaying state contents.

teaching_notes: Keep state content private; use supplied bucket/key/prefix permissions and approved/unapproved identities.

coverage.learning_objective: Configure locking for S3 Terraform state

required_facts.statement: The S3 backend supports lock-file locking when use_lockfile = true; locking is opt-in.
Set use_lockfile = true in the supplied S3 backend configuration and use the supplied s3:GetObject, s3:PutObject and s3:DeleteObject permissions on the .tflock object.
During the controlled state-changing operation that holds the lock, attempt a competing operation and verify it cannot acquire the lock or change state; do not disable locking to bypass the test.
Locking coordinates concurrent state writers; it is not an authorization boundary against identities that can directly change state objects.

misconceptions.statement: Force-unlock is not a safe way to bypass another active state writer; it is reserved for a lock from a failed operation when automatic unlocking failed.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: Two authorized Terraform operations must not change shared state at the same time. Enable the S3 lock-file mechanism and test contention without bypassing another active writer.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: The S3 backend supports lock-file locking when use_lockfile = true; locking is opt-in.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Set use_lockfile = true in the supplied S3 backend configuration and use the supplied s3:GetObject, s3:PutObject and s3:DeleteObject permissions on the .tflock object.

During the controlled state-changing operation that holds the lock, attempt a competing operation and verify it cannot acquire the lock or change state; do not disable locking to bypass the test.

Locking coordinates concurrent state writers; it is not an authorization boundary against identities that can directly change state objects.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Set use_lockfile = true in the supplied backend and grant the supplied GetObject, PutObject and DeleteObject permissions on the .tflock object. During the controlled state-changing operation holding the lock, start the supplied competing operation. Verify it cannot acquire the lock or change state. Do not disable locking to make the test proceed. If a lock remains from a failed operation and automatic unlocking failed, force-unlock has a specific recovery role; it is not a safe bypass for another active writer. Keep this coordination check distinct from tests of unauthorized direct state-object access.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: S3 lock-file locking is opt-in, not automatic for every backend. It coordinates concurrent writers and is not an authorization boundary. Force-unlock is reserved for a failed operation's leftover lock when automatic unlocking failed, not for bypassing an active writer.

teaching_blocks.title: A boundary that changes the interpretation
teaching_blocks.content: Force-unlock is not a safe way to bypass another active state writer; it is reserved for a lock from a failed operation when automatic unlocking failed.

video_need.reason: Two controlled authorized writers contending for the lock demonstrate serialization more clearly than a static backend setting.

media.group_title: Enable S3 lock-file locking and verify writer contention

segments.label: Enable locking and observe a competing Terraform apply being blocked
segments.summary: The presenter enables S3 lock-file locking with use_lockfile = true and reinitializes the backend. During an apply awaiting approval, the S3 bucket contains a .tflock object. After the operation completes, the state object remains and the lock object is gone. The demonstration then destroys and recreates its example infrastructure. While the next apply awaits approval, a second terminal attempts another apply against the same state and receives an error acquiring the state lock. Once the first operation completes, the second terminal can retry successfully and reports that the infrastructure matches the configuration. The lock coordinates these Terraform operations; the demonstrated contention ends through normal completion, without disabling locking.

bridge_note.before: Watch for the opt-in use_lockfile setting, the temporary .tflock object, and the second terminal's lock-acquisition error. The demonstration uses different infrastructure; your supplied exercise provisions a separate S3 bucket.
bridge_note.after: The competing apply is blocked until the first operation finishes. The clip omits .tflock permissions and the authorization-boundary distinction; the text covers both, plus why force-unlock must not bypass an active writer.

practice_anchor.objective: Enable use_lockfile = true in the supplied initialized S3 backend, using the supplied permissions for the .tflock object. Reinitialize using the supplied procedure, then use the supplied Terraform configuration to provision one separate S3 exercise bucket. With supplied synchronization holding the first state-changing operation's lock, attempt the supplied competing operation and verify that it cannot acquire the lock or change state. Do not disable locking or force-unlock the active writer.
practice_anchor.success: The backend has lock-file locking enabled with the supplied s3:GetObject, s3:PutObject and s3:DeleteObject permissions on .tflock. Recorded test evidence shows the competing operation failed to acquire the held lock and made no state change. The authorized first operation completes normally and provisions the separate exercise bucket.

live_code.required_skill: Edit the supplied Terraform S3 backend's locking setting and execute supplied Terraform operations to verify controlled writer contention.
live_code.starter_state_intent: Provide an initialized S3 backend with locking not yet enabled, a ready Terraform configuration for one separate S3 exercise bucket, authorized operator sessions, supplied .tflock permissions, and a synchronization procedure that holds the first operation's lock while the second attempts to run.
live_code.observable_success: The backend configuration enables use_lockfile; the first operation holds a .tflock object; the competing operation reports a lock-acquisition failure without changing state; normal completion releases the lock and leaves the separate exercise bucket provisioned.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show two authorized Terraform terminals targeting the same state: the first operation holds the lock while the second reports a lock-acquisition failure. Pair this with the S3 object's presence during contention, its absence after normal completion, and evidence that the competing operation made no state change.

teaching_notes: Use current S3 .tflock behavior; do not introduce obsolete mandatory DynamoDB locking or active-writer bypass.

context.concept_name: Control environment promotion with a manual approval

coverage.learning_objective: Gate environment promotion with manual approval

required_facts.statement: A manual approval action stops pipeline progression until an authorized approver approves; rejection or expiration fails the action.
Place an approval action between staging and production with the supplied review link or revision context and authorized approver permissions.
Verify the pipeline stops at approval and advances only after approval of the intended execution and revision.

misconceptions.statement: Receiving an approval notification does not itself grant permission to approve the action; approval requires the appropriate authorization.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A production promotion needs an authorized decision for the exact staged revision. The approval notification and the approver's authority are separate from the pipeline's wait point.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: A manual approval action stops pipeline progression until an authorized approver approves; rejection or expiration fails the action.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Place an approval action between staging and production with the supplied review link or revision context and authorized approver permissions.

Verify the pipeline stops at approval and advances only after approval of the intended execution and revision.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Place the supplied manual approval between staging and production with its review link or revision context and designated approver permissions. Verify the pipeline stops at that action. After approval of the intended execution and revision, verify it advances. Rejection or expiration fails the action. Receiving a notification does not itself grant permission to approve, so check the authorized approver rather than treating every recipient as eligible.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: A notification is not approval authority, and approval of one revision is not the recorded approval of another. Verify the intended execution/revision stops and advances only after its authorized approval.

teaching_blocks.title: A boundary that changes the interpretation
teaching_blocks.content: Receiving an approval notification does not itself grant permission to approve the action; approval requires the appropriate authorization.

video_need.reason: A short revision-specific approval pause and authorized decision helps verify progression while text covers the approval boundary.

practice_anchor.objective: Add one manual approval action between staging and production in the supplied pipeline, using the supplied review link or revision context and designated approver permissions.
practice_anchor.success: The approval action sits between staging and production and carries the supplied review context. The intended execution and revision stop at approval, production does not begin while approval is pending, and progression resumes only after the authorized approver accepts that execution and revision.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the staging-to-approval-to-production sequence visible, including the pending approval state, supplied review context, intended execution and revision, and production progression after authorized approval.

teaching_notes: Use supplied approval context and permissions; do not invent expiration durations or approvers.

context.concept_name: Recover an incident safely using an established runbook

coverage.learning_objective: Recover an incident using an established runbook

required_facts.statement: A runbook describes known procedures and their expected operational outcomes.
Verify the established runbook’s preconditions, execute only the approved actions and check each expected result before advancing.
On a supplied stop condition or an outcome outside the runbook’s bounds, stop routine execution and escalate with the observed evidence.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An incident matches an established runbook, but routine execution still depends on its preconditions and expected outcomes. Keep verification and stop decisions at each action boundary.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: A runbook describes known procedures and their expected operational outcomes.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Verify the established runbook’s preconditions, execute only the approved actions and check each expected result before advancing.

On a supplied stop condition or an outcome outside the runbook’s bounds, stop routine execution and escalate with the observed evidence.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Check the supplied runbook's preconditions before taking the first approved action. Execute only the stated approved steps and compare each actual result with its expected operational outcome before advancing. If a supplied stop condition occurs or a result falls outside the runbook's bounds, stop routine execution and escalate with the observed evidence. Record the last completed action and the result that required escalation so the next responder need not guess what happened. This example applies a known procedure safely; it does not authorize improvising further resource changes because the initial diagnosis seemed familiar.

For a passing step, record the actual result that matches the runbook before moving to the next approved action. For a failing step, preserve its output and stop/escalate according to the bounds. These branches keep the response reproducible for another operator. A runbook that initially fits the incident does not authorize continuing after its own expected-result check says the situation is outside routine execution.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: A known runbook is not unconditional permission to continue. Preconditions, expected results and stop bounds govern execution. An out-of-bounds result calls for stopping and escalation with evidence, not an unapproved extension of the procedure.

video_need.reason: One established runbook execution with expected-result and stop checks benefits from a controlled incident-response demonstration.

practice_anchor.objective: Respond to one seeded sandbox service incident using a supplied established runbook and escalation owner. Verify its preconditions, execute only approved actions, and compare each result with its expected outcome before advancing. Stop and escalate with observed evidence if a supplied stop condition occurs.
practice_anchor.success: The action record shows verified preconditions and only approved actions, with each expected-result check completed before advancement. Execution ends either with the runbook's recovery success checks satisfied or with routine execution stopped at a supplied stop condition or out-of-bounds result and an escalation containing the last completed action and observed evidence.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the supplied runbook's preconditions, approved current action, expected outcome, actual result, and stop condition visible alongside the execution record and recovery or escalation status.

teaching_notes: Use established runbook and owners; do not invent recovery actions or skip expected-result checks.

context.concept_name: Verify restored service and data against RTO/RPO in an isolated rehearsal

coverage.learning_objective: Verify restored service against RTO and RPO

required_facts.statement: Recovery verification must test both restoration time against RTO and recoverable data loss against RPO.
Using the supplied timestamps, measure elapsed time from the defined disruption start to passing service-readiness checks and compare it with RTO.

Using the supplied recovery markers, measure the gap between the disruption point and the latest recovered data point and compare it with RPO; a running service alone does not prove either objective was met.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An isolated rehearsal restored a service, but the recovery objectives need two separate measured comparisons. Use the defined disruption start, readiness result and recovered data markers to test RTO and RPO.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: Recovery verification must test both restoration time against RTO and recoverable data loss against RPO.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Using the supplied timestamps, measure elapsed time from the defined disruption start to passing service-readiness checks and compare it with RTO.

Using the supplied recovery markers, measure the gap between the disruption point and the latest recovered data point and compare it with RPO; a running service alone does not prove either objective was met.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: For an illustrative rehearsal, suppose disruption starts at 10:00 and the supplied readiness checks pass at 10:18. Elapsed restoration time is 18 minutes; compare that with the stated RTO, not with the data marker. If the latest recovered marker is 09:56, the gap from the 10:00 disruption point is 4 minutes; compare that with the stated RPO. With example objectives of 20 minutes RTO and 5 minutes RPO, both comparisons pass. If the marker were 09:50 instead, the service could still pass the time comparison while failing the data-loss comparison. These numbers are illustrative measurements, not AWS defaults. Retain the timestamps, marker and readiness evidence for both conclusions.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: A running service alone does not prove either objective was met. Measure elapsed time to passing readiness checks for RTO and the recovered-data gap for RPO. A good result for one cannot substitute for the other.

video_need.reason: A timestamped restoration/data-marker comparison clarifies independent RTO and RPO measurements and pass/fail conclusions.

practice_anchor.objective: Measure one isolated restoration using supplied disruption-start and passing-readiness timestamps, the latest recovered data marker, and stated RTO and RPO limits. Record each measured interval and its independent pass/fail conclusion.
practice_anchor.success: The completed worksheet measures restoration time from disruption start to passing service-readiness checks and compares it with RTO. It measures the gap from the latest recovered data marker to the disruption point and compares it with RPO. Both conclusions cite the supplied evidence rather than running-service status alone.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the two independent comparisons visible: disruption at 10:00 to passing readiness at 10:18 gives 18 minutes against a 20-minute RTO; a recovered marker at 09:56 gives a 4-minute gap against a 5-minute RPO. Include an alternative 09:50 marker to show that RPO can fail while RTO still passes.

teaching_notes: Use isolated rehearsal and supplied readiness/data markers; do not substitute resource status for service checks.

context.concept_name: Document incident evidence and a preventive change using reused systematic-debugging coverage

coverage.learning_objective: Document incident evidence and a preventive change

required_facts.statement: Post-incident analysis documents the incident’s impact, events, contributing causes and actions to reduce recurrence.
Write a timeline from supplied evidence and distinguish direct observations from causal conclusions supported by the verified fix.
Record one preventive action justified by the demonstrated cause, with an accountable owner and a way to verify completion.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A verified incident fix should lead to a factual timeline and one justified preventive action. Keep observations separate from causal conclusions so the follow-up does not overstate what the evidence established.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: Post-incident analysis documents the incident’s impact, events, contributing causes and actions to reduce recurrence.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Write a timeline from supplied evidence and distinguish direct observations from causal conclusions supported by the verified fix.

Record one preventive action justified by the demonstrated cause, with an accountable owner and a way to verify completion.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Write the timeline from the supplied timestamps and observations: symptom, investigation evidence, approved correction and verified result. State which causal conclusion the verified fix supports rather than treating every nearby event as a contributing cause. Record one preventive action tied to that demonstrated cause, name its accountable owner and state how completion will be checked. If the evidence supports only one narrow cause, keep the action equally bounded. The post-incident analysis should describe impact, events, contributing causes and recurrence-reduction work, not assign unsupported blame or add unrelated improvements.

A justified preventive action should close the demonstrated recurrence path. If the verified fix supports a particular configuration error, tie the one follow-up action to preventing or detecting that error rather than selecting an unrelated improvement. The owner and verification method make the action accountable. Keep the incident timeline factual even when a causal conclusion remains narrower than the team first suspected.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: A plausible causal story is not the same as a supported conclusion. Separate direct observations from conclusions backed by the verified fix, and give the justified preventive action an owner and verification method.

video_need.reason: A short observation/conclusion/action table helps tie one preventive change to verified evidence; text fully describes the analysis boundary.

media.group_title: Evidence-based incident records and accountable prevention

segments.label: Structure a factual incident record and accountable preventive actions
segments.summary: Post-incident analysis, called a postmortem here, records impact, response actions, causes and follow-up work. A blameless account focuses on contributing system and process conditions rather than accusing individuals or teams. A useful structure includes an executive summary, incident details, impact, causes and trigger, a timeline, lessons learned and action items. Severity claims should use verifiable data rather than dramatic language. Follow-up actions need clear owners, priorities, tracking tickets and verifiable completion criteria. Include prevention rather than only mitigation, and track completion dates or estimates so actions can be reviewed later.

bridge_note.before: Watch for the incident-record structure and concrete completion criteria for follow-up actions. The clip uses “postmortem” for post-incident analysis and emphasizes contributing causes rather than personal blame.
bridge_note.after: The clip explains structure and accountability, but does not work through an evidence timeline or justify one action from a verified cause. The text covers observation-versus-conclusion separation and cause-linked prevention.

practice_anchor.objective: Write one short incident record using supplied logs, impact evidence and a verified fix. Include a factual timeline, a separately identified supported causal conclusion and one justified preventive action with an accountable owner and completion check.
practice_anchor.success: The record documents impact and timestamped events without inventing evidence, distinguishes observations from the causal conclusion supported by the verified fix, and ties one preventive action to that demonstrated cause. The action names an accountable owner and a verifiable completion condition.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the evidence-to-action link visible in a table containing supplied timestamps and direct observations, the causal conclusion supported by the verified fix, and one justified preventive action with its owner and completion check.

teaching_notes: Use supplied evidence only; do not invent causal facts, blame or unrelated preventive work.

coverage.learning_objective: Cut over a recovered service endpoint

required_facts.statement: Recovery procedures include restoring service and directing clients to the recovered environment.
Confirm the restored target’s supplied readiness checks pass, perform the approved DNS or application endpoint switch and verify clients reach the restored target.
For DNS cutover, account for cached answers and TTL when testing client convergence rather than assuming every client immediately uses the new endpoint.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A restored target has passed its readiness checks, and clients now need to reach it through the approved endpoint change. Verify convergence rather than assuming every client immediately follows the new setting.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: Recovery procedures include restoring service and directing clients to the recovered environment.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Confirm the restored target’s supplied readiness checks pass, perform the approved DNS or application endpoint switch and verify clients reach the restored target.

For DNS cutover, account for cached answers and TTL when testing client convergence rather than assuming every client immediately uses the new endpoint.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Confirm the restored target's supplied readiness checks before the approved DNS or application-endpoint switch. Perform that switch through the supplied procedure and test that clients reach the restored target. For a DNS switch, account for cached answers and TTL while checking client convergence. A changed DNS setting and an old client answer can coexist during caching; retain the actual client-target evidence instead of declaring all clients moved at the update request.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Endpoint configuration is not the same as verified client convergence. For DNS, cached answers and TTL matter; test clients reaching the ready restored target rather than assuming an immediate universal switch.

video_need.reason: A short ready-target cutover and client-cache timeline helps explain DNS convergence without implying an immediate universal switch.

practice_anchor.objective: Use a supplied sandbox cutover procedure to confirm the restored service's readiness checks pass, switch one supplied DNS endpoint to that service, and verify client convergence using the supplied TTL and client-target evidence.
practice_anchor.success: The endpoint switch occurs only after readiness checks pass and through the approved procedure. Client checks establish that clients reach the restored target, accounting for cached DNS answers and the supplied TTL rather than treating the configuration update as immediate convergence.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show the restored target passing readiness checks before the approved DNS switch, followed by a client-convergence timeline distinguishing the updated endpoint setting from clients retaining cached answers until their supplied TTL expires.

teaching_notes: Use approved cutover procedure only after readiness; do not invent DNS record commands or TTL defaults.
